family_judgments.evidence: Cloze, dialogue completion, multiple choice, and transformation are all familiar ways to practise the same short offer.
Every item repeats the same cold room, open window, and “Shall I close the window?” response, so the four formats provide limited meaningful variation.

criteria.evidence: The instruction specifies the required words and the blank leads directly into “the window?”.
A short-text field before the fixed ending supports entering “Shall I close”.
“room,” “cold,” “window,” “open,” and “close” are familiar, concrete vocabulary for B2 learners.
Offering to close an open window because the room is cold is a natural everyday situation.
The constrained prompt gives substantial support while still requiring correct question word order.
The task is short, clearly scorable, and suitable for a standard fill-in response field.
The dialogue establishes the problem and asks the learner to complete Maya’s reply as an offer.
The incomplete labelled turn makes it clear that the learner should type Maya’s next utterance.
The dialogue uses simple everyday language, including “getting cold” and “window”.
Maya’s proposed reply follows naturally from Leo saying that it is cold.
At B2, producing a short conventional offer from an explicit dialogue context is plausible.
A single-turn free-text dialogue completion is readily presented and scored in a simple practice interface.
The stem and instruction clearly ask what Maya should say to make an offer.
The four labelled sentence options fit a conventional single-choice interaction.
All options use familiar vocabulary and preserve the same concrete situation.
The stated reason for the offer gives the learner enough pragmatic context to select the appropriate sentence.
The distractors contrast recognizable word-order and verb-form errors, making this a plausible supported B2 check.
It is an immediately deployable multiple-choice item with one unambiguous correct option.
The source sentence, stated communicative purpose, and cue words clearly indicate the required rewrite.
A full-sentence entry field is appropriate for a rewrite that includes a question mark.
The source and cue contain only common words such as “can,” “close,” and “window”.
Changing “I can close the window” into an offer is meaningful in the supplied cold-room context.
The cue strongly constrains the response but still requires the learner to form the offer as a question.
The required response is explicit and can be scored reliably as a short constructed sentence.

summary: The formats are clear and deployable; the main product concern is the highly repetitive scenario and target sentence across the family.
